title: System Binary Proxy Execution: CMSTP
summary: CMSTP.exe, the Microsoft Connection Manager Profile Installer, is a command-line program that installs Connection Manager service profiles used for remote access connections, and it takes an installation information file, an INF, as its input. An adversary supplies a crafted INF in which commands are hidden in the sections CMSTP processes during installation, and the tool runs them. The same mechanism can point CMSTP at a remote library file or a COM scriptlet to load and execute, in a manner comparable to the scriptlet abuse seen with Regsvr32. CMSTP also exposes an auto-elevated COM interface, so it can raise its own privileges and execute arbitrary commands from the malicious INF without a consent prompt, which makes it relevant to user account control bypass as well as to execution. Because the binary is legitimate and may be signed by Microsoft, application control solutions that do not account for it can be bypassed. Detection evidence includes CMSTP process creation with an INF path in a temporary, download or public folder, an unmanaged command line using silent switches, CMSTP as the parent of a command shell, script host or registration utility, and network connections from CMSTP fetching remote content. Legitimate use is an administrator installing a managed connection profile from a trusted location, with no child process and no unexpected traffic.

beginner.definition: CMSTP is a Windows program that installs connection profiles, which the system uses for remote access connections. It reads a setup file with the ending .inf that describes what the connection needs. The program is signed by Microsoft, so many tools trust it.
beginner.whyItMatters: A setup file can hide commands that run during installation. CMSTP can also raise its own rights, so those commands may run as an administrator. The user sees no permission window at all, which makes the attack hard to spot. If you ignore this, a simple file download can become full control of the machine.
howItWorks: The program cmstp.exe installs connection profiles, which Windows uses for remote access connections.
It reads a setup file ending in .inf that lists what the connection needs and what to run.
An attacker writes a setup file that hides commands in the section cmstp runs during installation.
Because the program starts with high rights by itself, the commands it runs also receive those rights.
The setup file can also point at a library file or a script on an internet server, which cmstp then loads.
The user never sees a permission window, so the elevation happens silently and is easy to miss.
beginner.example: A building has a service lift that cleaners and engineers use every day. An engineer's key opens the machine room without asking the front desk for anything. Someone copies that key and rides the service lift all the way to the roof. The front desk log shows nothing unusual, because no permission was ever requested. The service key is the silent elevation, and the machine room is the access an attacker wants.
takeaways: cmstp.exe can raise its own rights, so it may run code as an administrator without any prompt.
Watch for setup files in user folders and for cmstp.exe starting other programs.
Installing a connection profile should be a planned task, never a surprise.

objectives: Explain what a Connection Manager service profile is and what CMSTP does with an INF file.
Describe how an INF file can carry commands that CMSTP executes during installation.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the System Binary Proxy Execution parent technique.
Explain why CMSTP can elevate privileges without showing a consent prompt.
Identify the process and network evidence that indicates CMSTP abuse rather than routine profile installation.
